Everful , a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.
The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.
Everful is on track to reach $100 million in annualized revenue by the end of the year, about two and a half years after its launch, co-founder Sisi Song said. The company ships over 5 million items a month to customers in more than 60 countries and works with over 30,000 factory partners, she added. Its online wholesale catalog includes more than 20 million products.
Song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous company to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024. The company began as a jewelry wholesale business before evolving into a multi-category, factory-direct sourcing platform.
Retailers and brands often rely on intermediaries, face high minimum order requirements, and experience long sourcing cycles, which tie up capital in inventory before sales trends are clear. Song noticed the growing gap between fast-changing consumer trends and traditional wholesale sourcing models while working as a venture investor at Bessemer Venture Partners, where she mostly focused on cross-border sourcing and meeting numerous startups in the sector. That same gap shaped Everful’s goal to simplify buying directly from factories through an AI-enabled platform.
The B2B sourcing industry is highly competitive. Big tech giant Alibaba connects international buyers with manufacturers and suppliers, while Faire, a San Francisco-based wholesale tech platform, enables retailers to purchase wholesale inventory directly from brands. According to Everful’s co-founders, its key differentiator is responsibility for the sourcing process, rather than simply facilitating transactions.
“We take care of everything,” Han said. “We handle sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. That’s something the marketplaces don’t offer.”
Everful is built for smaller retailers and brands without dedicated sourcing teams, Song said, and it also verifies the factories it works with. While peers also offer services such as quality inspection, logistics, and AI-powered sourcing, Everful aims to integrate these capabilities into a more streamlined purchasing experience, creating an end-to-end process that reduces the work retailers must handle themselves.
Han added that Everful uses AI agents to automate labor-intensive sourcing tasks, including tracking consumer trends, identifying suppliers, coordinating orders across factories, and managing logistics.
Because Everful sources from Chinese factories, ongoing U.S.-China trade tensions and tariffs bear directly on its business. Song said the co-founders have been thinking about geopolitical issues since day one of building the company, and that this has shaped Everful’s strategy from the outset, leveraging her experience at Alibaba and Bessemer Venture Partners.
She mentioned the Trump administration’s suspension of the de minimis exemption , which had allowed eligible shipments valued at $800 or less to enter the U.S. duty-free, as one example of a shift in trade policy.
Song explained such changes could favor a model that combines overseas sourcing with local retail sales. “We’re empowering local retailers and brands,” she said. “Long-term cross-border commerce will be cross-border B2B sourcing plus local selling.”
Everful plans to use the Series A round to expand its presence in the U.S. and Europe, particularly the U.K., France, and Italy, while investing in AI to automate product customization and other sourcing workflows. It also aims to deepen integrations with e-commerce platforms, building on its Shopify integration as it works toward becoming an end-to-end infrastructure platform for global sourcing.
The startup employs about 70 full-time staff globally, including 45 in research and development. It has also established an AI operations team to connect engineering and business functions.

Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.
Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies , a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking , this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.
Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.
“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”
So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.
As the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”
Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services , for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.
In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.
On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.
It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.
Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS , Google Cloud Platform , and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products , Google Workspace , telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.
When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the Internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon —but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net . Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts .
When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off Internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.
Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what’s actually going on,” she says.
Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.
Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that …

The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information.
The Thursday ruling from the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret.
The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
The ruling comes a year after the U.K. government reportedly demanded that Apple build a backdoor to allow U.K. authorities access to customer data anywhere in the world. Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort , arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk.
California-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order.
Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. A spokesperson for Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment following the ruling, but previously told TechCrunch that the company has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.”
A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment.
Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order.
A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.

As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models , they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.
“Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea . That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.
The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks , to test their defenses.
“Agents are not programmed so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see, the exploration space that we have to address is huge and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgement when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”
Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.
Even though the entire environment is controlled by Google, Chrome is built with so many user protections and validity checks that in order to allow the agents to use real Chrome (which is crucial for accurate training), the researchers essentially had to hack the browser and take elaborate steps like making forged web certificates for validity checks so the agents could have a normal experience. The team emphasizes, though, that none of these attacks would be possible against regular Chrome users on the open internet. They were all facilitated by the god-mode type access and privilege the team inherently has because they control the entire environment and network.
The researchers say that while the browsing assistant agents they have been testing are benign and do not have cyber capabilities, their goal is to make the Mirror Dimension available to teams across Google so more researchers have access to the safe and controlled environment for testing.
“We’re sharing this approach so other teams both internally and externally think about doing it this way,” says Doug Turner, Google’s director of engineering. “This is the first step, there’s going to be continued investment in this approach to train models. And I would imagine as they become more sophisticated we’ll have to continue working on this environment to make it more and more realistic.”

The International Court of Justice has found Myanmar guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority. It is the first time in the court’s 80-year history that it has ruled a state committed the crime.
"The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said on Thursday, reading the verdict in The Hague, Netherlands.
For almost three hours, Iwasawa set out the evidence from the military’s 2017 campaign against the mostly Muslim Rohingya, which drove hundreds of thousands of people across the border into Bangladesh.
He said Myanmar's security forces had killed thousands of Rohingya civilians and committed "widespread sexual violence" against women and "extreme violence" against children.
The judges found that Rohingya villages had been systematically destroyed and resettled with non-Rohingya people. They concluded that the "only reasonable inference" was that Myanmar intended to destroy the group, which is the legal test for genocide.
The court ordered Myanmar to compensate the Rohingya for "the damage caused by the violations of its obligations... in so far as such damage is not made good by restitution". The amount will be decided at a later date.
Myanmar must also "allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return" of those who fled, and investigate and punish anyone suspected of taking part in the genocide.
ICJ rulings are binding and cannot be appealed. However, the court has no power to enforce them, and it is unclear whether Myanmar’s leaders will comply.
The verdict is likely to add to pressure on Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military during the 2017 crackdown. He seized power from Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in a 2021 coup, and this year he was installed as civilian president after tightly restricted elections. The ruling could complicate his push for international recognition.
Agnes Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International, called the ruling "a historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families".
Legal experts are watching the case for signs of how the ICJ might rule on South Africa's separate case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
More than a million Rohingya now live in the world’s largest refugee camp, across the border in Bangladesh. Refugees there have described gang rapes, mass executions and attacks on families and children.
"I want justice," said a 23-year-old survivor of rape, speaking to AFP before the verdict from the cramped shelter she shares with her family. She asked not to be named.
"There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women," she said.
Mohammed Osman, 20, said he hoped the ruling would let him go home to perform last rites for his parents and younger brother, who were killed by the military.
"They shot my father dead, forced my mother into a house with a few other women, raped them and burnt down our homestead," he told AFP.
The Gambia brought the case in 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which allows any signatory state to take another to court over suspected breaches. It has the backing of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
"It is not about esoteric issues of international law, it is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings," said Dawda Jallow, The Gambia’s justice minister.
Myanmar has always denied genocide. It says it was responding to an insurgency after militant attacks killed about a dozen members of its security forces.
"Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein," Ko Ko Hlaing, Myanmar’s representative, told the judges at hearings in January.

Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home ⁠of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence.
Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a ​week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support ‌for Hasina’s planned return in December , culminating in a ‌nationwide lockdown on Thursday.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent ⁠protests demanding her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card to facilitate her return. Her supporters are protesting against the government’s rejection of that request.
To deter ⁠violence, 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard fanned out across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, considered to have many Hasina supporters, a spokesperson ⁠said.
Police said former interim leader Yunus’ ancestral home in Chattogram, about 300km (186 miles) south-east of Dhaka, ​was set on fire late on ‌Wednesday.
It is likely that flammable ‌substances were thrown into an unused ground-floor room, police told Reuters, adding that Yunus’ paternal family members, who live on the upper floors, are safe.
Reuters could not immediately reach the Yunus Centre thinktank that speaks on his behalf to seek comment. Yunus and his government, which led Bangladesh after Hasina’s ouster, have faced hostility from her supporters.
During the last 10 days of protests, police have reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of ‌vehicles being set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public, media have said.
Late on Tuesday, an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest near Hasina’s home district of Gopalganj, police said.
On the same night, a crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of cultural affairs minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and shops ‌belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district of Pirojpur after two buses ​were set on fire, authorities said.
Tuesday marks a year since Hasina was ​sentenced to death by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising against her in 2024. She has lived in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka.
On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, who faces charges ⁠over several killings during the 2024 protests, from his house in Dhaka, police told Reuters.
At ​least 37 branches and offices of ​Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, have been targeted in arson attacks or ​attempted fires since 10 November, ‌with 14 more ​attacked since midnight ​on Tuesday, the bank said.
On Tuesday, the home minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved in violence would be identified and prosecuted.
Awami League leaders, most of them in hiding, could not be reached for comment.

The much-expected, unprecedented trilateral meeting of US President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin concluded with a "peace declaration" focusing on UN reforms, fuel supplies and reducing nuclear risks, but it did not mention the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
Against the backdrop of powerful, historic imagery of the three global powers, the summit appears not to have produced immediate diplomatic breakthroughs, ending without joint statements, despite strong declarations by the leaders at the beginning, and with US President Trump immediately departing the venue for the airport.
A video released by the Kremlin showed Putin telling Xi, “Thank you for organising this, I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well,” as Xi accompanied him to the car after the summit.
Chinese state media and Russian officials released a joint statement called the "trilateral peace declaration," in which Xi, Putin and Trump said that they are committed to upholding strategic stability and international security.
According to the statement, China, Russia and the US agreed on UN reforms, boosting production and supply of petroleum products, engaging in dialogue to reduce nuclear risks, and "respect for the immunity of state officials and opposition to the ICC and similar institutions abusing their jurisdiction."
The declaration makes no explicit reference to Ukraine, Iran, North Korea or other issues.
Going into the meeting and in his pre-summit bilateral talks with Putin and Xi, Trump said he wanted to talk about reducing nuclear stockpiles, Russia’s war in Ukraine and “all of the problems that are really being discussed in the world.”
With the Russian state apparatus projecting Putin's participation in the summit as a major legitimisation win, the Russian president was the first of the three leaders to hold a news conference for Russian media after the meeting.
The Russian president said that the summit was an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy" and that "the discussion took place in a completely open atmosphere, which allowed us to understand one another better," adding that "overall, it was very useful."
Putin said that he and Trump have a "certain closeness" in their views and "on civilisational values."
Addressing the topic of Russia's ongoing all-out war in Ukraine, Putin said that Kyiv and Europe are not yet ready to make compromises to end it.
At the start of the summit, Putin said that Russia’s war in Ukraine would be part of the talks, stating that “we have shared interests in Ukraine.” However, after the meeting, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the Russian media that Ukraine was not "the central topic" at the summit.
“Russia, the US and China are united not only by their status as victorious nations in World War II, but also by their responsibility for maintaining international peace,” Putin said before the talks.
China's president Xi Jinping described the summit as "positive, constructive and fruitful," according to a Chinese state media report.
According to the report, Xi said they agreed that major powers should take the legitimate security concerns of all countries seriously, stating that "as long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace.”
“The seeds planted at today’s trilateral meeting will surely take root, sprout, blossom and bear fruit,” Xi was quoted as saying.
The three leaders posed for a family photo without shaking hands as they started their summit and made no joint statements when it concluded after an hour and 20 minutes.
During joint statements before the summit, Trump said the three global powers "are making history" as they have "great responsibilities to solve problems that affect the entire planet."
Xi joined Trump in saying their summit “has groundbreaking significance”, adding that “the world is at peace when great powers live in harmony," calling on the three countries to “abandon Cold War mentality, not pursue decoupling and breaking chains”.
"The three countries should work together to address global challenges,” and that "major countries should respect each other, coexist peacefully,” Xi said before the talks began, concluding that they "can strengthen coordination to safeguard global energy supply chain stability. “Adversity reveals true responsibility.”
Just as the summit was starting, China's state news agency published a statement from Xi saying that “nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, building a nuclear-free world.”
In the statement, Xi described nuclear weapons as "the sword of Damocles hanging over humanity", and that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought."
In his opening statements, Trump said that the “three countries are uniquely positioned to discuss nuclear weapons" and "to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world."
“Too often past leaders avoided talking to leaders they had disagreements with,” Trump added.
The US and Chinese presidents met bilaterally earlier on Thursday in their third substantial meeting this year.
During the meeting, Trump said that the US and China want to help end the war in Ukraine, stating that "we're looking to both help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine."
The US president praised their friendship and their shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, which has become a key site of attacks in the Iran war.
Xi said that relations between the US and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump’s presidency.
“The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi said.
Trump also met Putin ahead of the trilateral, stating that “we’ve had a great relationship for many years.”
Their meeting marks the first time the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia's war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start,” Trump said as he greeted Putin, saying "Who is he? He's my friend."
The summit has stoked fears that the three powerful men may seek to divide the globe into spheres of influence, for example by making decisions that affect Ukraine's fate over the heads of Kyiv or Europe.
France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot reacted to the French media after the Shenzhen summit by saying that "these three leaders fundamentally disagree on everything, so they cannot agree on anything.”
“As for this photograph that has generated so much discussion, it isn’t quite a photograph of the world’s three greatest powers, because the world’s three greatest powers are the United States, of course, China and the European Union,” the French foreign minister told RTL radio.

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has rejected the UK government’s attempt to keep its order secret, marking a significant victory for transparency.
There's something pretty extraordinary about a government being able to demand changes to the security of devices used by millions of people, prevent a company that makes those devices from discussing those demands, and then refuse to even acknowledge that the demands exist at all.
That has been the sordid situation surrounding the UK governement's ongoing dispute with Apple over encrypted iCloud data. Up until today, the UK government's position has essentially been that it would neither confirm nor deny whether it issued Apple with a Technical Capability Notice (TCN). These are secret orders issued under Section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 , which gives the UK government powers to require technology companies to make changes to their services to facilitate the exercise of investigatory powers. Today, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal has ruled that the UK government must acknowledge that it issued Apple with such a notice .
This is a big deal. Whilst it doesn't mean we suddenly know everything the UK government wants Apple to do, the government's attempt to keep even the existence of the order secret has now suffered a major defeat.
I covered the background to this extensively in my piece, Two-Tier Encryption in the UK . The story goes back to February 2025 when the Washington Post exposed that the government had ordered Apple to provide ‘backdoor’ access to encrypted iCloud data, belonging not just to users in the UK, but around the world. The order was reportedly issued in January 2025 under the Investigatory Powers Act — the centrepiece of the UK’s modern surveillance law.
Rather than weaken its security provisions, Apple took the quite extraordinary step of withdrawing Advanced Data Protection (ADP) from new UK users. ADP is an optional feature that extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data — when enabled, even Apple can't decrypt the protected information. [1] Apple subsequently made clear that it would not build a backdoor or a master key into any of its products or services . They stated this without publicly referencing the Technical Capability Notice, as they were forbidden from doing so.
The original order's scope extended beyond British users — it potentially implicated the encrypted data of Apple's customers all around the world, including the United States. Following months of diplomatic wrangling involving the Trump administration, the UK government withdrew that original notice , but that wasn't the end of it. The UK government issued a second Technical Capability Notice , this time reportedly restricted to British users. Apple's original legal challenge was subsequently dismissed following with the withdrawal of the first notice, so the company launched a fresh legal challenge in 2026 .
The difficulty for the UK government has always been that the existence of the original order was already widely reported. The Washington Post had published its exposé, and many other news outlets subsequently reported on it. The UK government nevertheless maintained its position of neither confirming nor denying the existence of individual TCNs.
At a hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on 17 September this year, lawyers representing civil rights organisations Liberty and Privacy International challenged that position. Ben Jaffey KC, representing the organisations, argued that the UK government's insistence on maintaining secrecy had become increasingly difficult to justify. Jaffey compared the secrecy order to the “emperor’s new clothes… and brings the administration of justice into disrepute” .
The existence of the order was already public knowledge and continuing to pretend otherwise was obstructing the proper consideration of the legal challenge. The UK government disagreed, arguing that abandoning its neither-confirm-nor-deny policy could damage national security by assisting hostile actors in building a picture of which companies were subject to such notices. Today the tribunal rejected that argument.
“The respondent has not established that it would be damaging to national security to reveal in these proceedings, as is the case, that the respondent has given Apple a Technical Capability Notice.”
The Tribunal hasn't ruled that the underlying order was unlawful; it hasn't made a determination whether the UK government can legitimately require Apple to make changes to its encryption systems; it hasn't disclosed the precise technical requirements of the notice. But the government has lost an important argument about keeping the proceedings secret.
In my Two-Tier Encryption in the UK piece, I used the idea of “Alice and Bill”, two fictional people living in the UK, both using identical iPhones and both paying for iCloud, to illustrate a fundamental problem that had arisen from the dispute between Apple and the UK government.
Alice had enabled Advanced Data Protection before Apple withdrew the feature for new UK users , Bill hadn't. Alice continued to benefit from Apple's strongest available iCloud encryption protections, Bill couldn't even enable them. The result was a peculiar situation in which two customers using the same service had materially different levels of protection.
Because Apple withdrew ADP for new UK users in February 2025, existing users who had already enabled the feature have not since been required to turn it off — Apple’s security documentation says its servers can’t modify the ADP setting, or roll it back on a user’s behalf. This has created a ‘two-tier’ system of protection based on when somebody enabled a particular security feature.
Our iCloud accounts contain a lot of private information — photos, documents, backups, other material that most of us reasonably expect to remain fully private. Encryption exists so that the service provider shouldn't have the ability to access that information. If a government can compel a technology company to undermine its own protections, the consequences deserve considerably more scrutiny than secret exchanges between officials and lawyers. Today's ruling makes scrutiny more possible.
The Investigatory Powers Act doesn't only exist to regulate Apple's relationship with the UK government. Its provisions establish powers that can potentially be applied to other communications and technology providers. What happens when these powers are used against another company? What happens when the next notice concerns a different service or a different encryption system, or a different category of personal information? How would customers even know about it anyway? That's one of the most troubling aspects of the TCN regime - the secrecy . Companies receiving TCNs can be legally prohibited from disclosing that they have received them.
The UK government’s position, of course, is that these powers are necessary to support lawful investigations and protect public safety. Liberty and Privacy International have thankfully been challenging the lawfulness, necessity and secrecy of this regime. They argue it lacks adequate safeguards and threatens fundamental rights. Apple is pursuing its own legal challenge. These cases are now proceeding alongside one another with a substantive hearing expected sometime in 2027. Today's decision doesn't resolve the wider questions, but it does remove one obstacle to examining the dispute in public.
Apple has consistently argued that it will not build ‘backdoors’ into its products. The UK government, meanwhile, has relied on powers that allow it to issue orders to technology companies in secret. For now, the legal process has at least established that the government issued this particular order, but my guess is that we're still some distance from fully understanding what it actually wants Apple to do, and whether it has the legal authority to demand it.

The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let refugees return safely.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide .
The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state .
The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.
"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.
He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and if necessary prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.
The ICJ said that by its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.
Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.
"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But the court found that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and if anything fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.
At one point reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."
He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.
There was no immediate response from the government in Myanmar or the military that's seen as the real underlying power.
Rohingya activist Yasmin Ullah — a Canadian citizen since 2016 but who was born in Rakhine state and who was a member of Gambia's delegation that filed the ICJ case — called the verdict more important for the world than for her community.
"The Rohingya never needed a court to tell us what happened to us," she said. "We needed the world to hear it, and today it has."
Wai Wai Nu, a Rohingya activist who directs the Women's Peace Network NGO, said the world's highest court's finding followed "decades" when "the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence and dismiss our suffering."
And the co-chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council, Nay San Lwin, said that for Ronihgya, "justice means the restoration of our citizenship, recognition of our identity and our safe and dignified return home."
Myanmar's shadow national unity government, which includes remnants of former President Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy Party, said it "respects the authority" of the ICJ.
It said that since the beginning of the "revolution against military dictatorship" in 2021, it had affirmed its "commitment to the rule of law, human rights, justice and states' obligations to prevent and punish genocide."
Myanmar was under nominally civilian rule at the time of the atrocities but the extent to which President Aung San Suu Kyi's government held sway over the military and its actions is debatable.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres welcomed Thursday's verdict, calling it a "powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and noting it was the first verdict of its kind against a state.
"Myanmar must act in accordance with its obligation to comply with the Court's decision," Guterres said in a statement, adding that this includes "the safe, voluntary and dignified return [of Rohingya] to their place of residence nad reunification of families."
Gambia's Justice Minister Dawda Jallow, who attended the hearing, spoke to reporters afterwards at the Peace Palace in The Hague.
"The victory belongs to the Rohingya," Jallow said. "They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe."
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband issued a statement saying the former colonial power was "taking immediate action today in light of this judgment."
Miliband said Britain would expel Myanmar's defense attache in London and was calling for a special UN Security Council session in response. He called on Myanmar to "comply fully with the judgment," and on the international community to "play its part in supporting implementation, accountability, and justice for the Rohingya."
UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the ruling "clearly concludes the State of Myanmar stands responsible for one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind."
The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.
A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp .
Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.
Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.
Aung San Suu Kyi , who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
The case is likely to draw close attention from those pursuing ICJ prosecutions against Israel and Benjamin Netanyahu for the war in Gaza and against Russia and Vladimir Putin for the invasion of Ukraine.

Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.
Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.
The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.
Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.
The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.
The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.
But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.
One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.
Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.
But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.
Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".
In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.
Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.
The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei co-founded firm five years ago
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.
While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.
Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.
Anthropic was started by seven former OpenAI employees, led by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei.
Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the risks posed by AI, amounting in his view to a possible threat to human existence.
The company has called for a slowdown in the development of AI, and a greater focus on safeguards while forging ahead with plans to grow quickly and boost its financing through the public markets.
OpenAI has voiced similar sentiments and delayed its plans to list on the stock market in order to address AI safety concerns.
Technology stocks have lost value in recent weeks following the US midterm elections. Democrats, who now control of both chambers of Congress, are expected to be tougher on AI regulation. Some Democrat candidates opposed the rapid build of data centres required to run AI.
But Anthropic went ahead with its market listing, despite the market volatility, because it needed to tap into additional funds, said Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton told the BBC. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more and so the time has come."
Expensive computer chips, necessary for the industry to operate, are in short supply.
And the US Federal Reserve is concerned about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss interest rates, as well as the high concentration of AI exposure among a small number of firms.

Priced at $83 a share, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot raised over $80 billion and achieved a $1.5 trillion valuation on its Wall Street debut. Inside Nasdaq, co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the opening bell to celebrate the start of trading; outside, protesters chanted against the flotation and the concentration of tech-sector wealth in a demonstration that saw three people detained by police .
The listing overtook SpaceX’s blockbuster June offering , highlighting relentless investor enthusiasm for AI despite growing talk of overheated technology valuations. Robust demand carried the share price clear of its earlier $70 to $78 guide range . Yet demonstrators warned that ordinary investors could pay the price if the AI surge ends in a financial bust. Jose Gonzalez, among those protesting outside, questioned who would bear the brunt of a market reversal, arguing that wealthy investors enjoy protections unavailable to the public.
The meteoric surge of artificial intelligence is sparking hope and alarm in equal measure. While global spending on AI approaches $850 billion in 2026 and enthusiasts hail a sweeping economic and technological revolution, economists and watchdogs warn of a looming financial bubble, swelling debt and growing inequality, alongside fears that automation will wipe out jobs and funnel vast wealth into the coffers of a few tech titans.

Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility
The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.
It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen , and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
The gathering, which follows up last year’s inaugural EU-UK summit in London, was scheduled for July but postponed when Keir Starmer resigned.
The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were initiated under Starmer’s government.
First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports .
A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules.
The third deal is the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give those aged 18-30 the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – bad news for anyone in their late 20s.
With less than 24 hours before the summit begins, two big issues remain open. EU negotiators want to ensure EU students pay the UK rate of university tuition, around four or five times lower than international fees. The two sides also disagree over how many people would be allowed to take part: the EU wants 100,000 visas a year, but the UK is looking at 50,000 to 80,000 to keep migration numbers down.
To maximise its leverage on tuition fees, the EU is linking the three agreements, warning they must come into force together.
Not on Friday. The UK has been pushing for inclusion in the EU’s Made in Europe plan, a protectionist scheme to favour EU companies when public money is being spent on goods such as electric cars, renewable energy and nuclear technology. Inclusion in Made in Europe is a big priority for the Burnham government, which has dangled major concessions on tuition fees to make sure British firms are not shut out.
The problem for London is that the EU lawmakers have not finalised the Made in Europe law, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. Many EU member states want to include the UK, but France and the European parliament take a stricter position.
The EU law is not expected to be agreed until spring 2027. To help the British government, which has linked a generous offer on youth mobility with Made in Europe, the European Commission proposed delaying agreement on tuition fees by six months. But member states want precise guarantees now about equal treatment for EU students.
Another problem is that British inclusion in Made in Europe requires the UK to sign up to EU trade-defence policies. The EU, for instance, has imposed high tariffs on “unfairly subsidised” Chinese electric cars and fears the UK, which has not followed suit, could become an alternative route into the EU if Chinese companies set up in Britain and sell into the bloc. The EU is calling on the UK to align with its trade-defence policies, but the UK insists it can guard against circumvention without copying the EU.
In a sign of possible tensions, an earlier summit text proposing a trusted partnership on economic security has been downgraded to a partnership.
Beyond the headline deals, the EU-UK draft summit statement opens the door to British integration in European policies on energy, crime-fighting, educational exchange, tech and foreign policy cooperation.
The next major agreement, targeted for next year, is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. This is a priority for five EU member states : Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions.
Beyond that, the two sides will “explore opportunities” for the UK to join the Erasmus student exchange programme after 2027; the current arrangement applies only for the 2027-8 academic year .
In a win for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects. The sides will sign a digital partnership, which includes joint work on AI safety, and examine how to share data on law enforcement and border management.
Far from it. A lot of diplomatic plates are spinning, but the UK remains outside the EU’s biggest economic clubs: the single market and the customs union. It also has no decision-making powers inside the EU.
Burnham says he will set out the long-term options for the future relationship after this week’s summit. “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain,” he said on Monday in a major speech . But amid concerns among some cabinet ministers about reopening Brexit divides, the prime minister appears to be taking a more cautious approach. He said the process would take time and insisted that “at every stage the British people will be the boss”.
The EU has welcomed Britain’s interest in rejoining but is wary of a protracted negotiation that could be reversed by an anti-EU British government.
In an echo of the Brexit years, EU insiders say, once again, that it is up to Britain to define what it wants.

Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 19. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.
Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority. Myanmar's military-backed government has not yet responded to the ruling at the time of writing.
Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.
But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.
"I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."
For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.
The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.
Judges of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) attend a public hearing ahead of the reading of the court's judgment in the genocide case brought by Gambia against Myanmar, in The Hague on Thursday. Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.
"Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."
She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."
Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."
"We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."
Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.
"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.
Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar, on Thursday. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.
She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.
"Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.
The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.
In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.
Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.
The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.
The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.
However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.
The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.
Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.
Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.
Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.
"Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.
She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.

US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

The UK premier is heading to Brussels for the second round of EU talks aimed at deepening post-Brexit cooperation.
Lincolnshire, United Kingdom – A decade is a short time in cheesemaking. Barrels of Tim Jones’ “Lincolnshire Poachers” cheese rest on their racks for months and years, disturbed only by Florence, the robot cheese turner.
The most mature cheese in Tim’s Lincolnshire dairy, in the English midlands, is five years old. By that measure, it was only a couple of cheeses ago that 52 percent of the British public voted for the country’s most tumultuous constitutional revolt in living memory.
Jones was one of them. But he is under no illusion that it went well – particularly for his exports.
“It suddenly made life much harder. We lost certain customers, and it became more expensive to get the cheese there. It definitely harmed our business,” he told Al Jazeera.
Ten years after the UK voted to leave the European Union, few are happy with what they got.
Remainers are still heartbroken that a majority of the country did not look on EU membership with approval. Leavers, by and large, think many of Brexit’s promised benefits were never delivered.
“I did vote to leave,” said Jones. “But I didn’t vote to leave in the way that we did.”
Recent polling tells a consistent story: A majority of Britons now view Brexit as a mistake.
In September, 55 percent of respondents told YouGov that leaving the EU was a wrong turn for the UK. Only 21 percent think it was the right decision.
The relatively new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has noticed the shift in public mood. Less cautious than his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Burnham reignited the Brexit debate shortly after taking office in July.
He has ruled out major changes to the UK’s relationship with the EU before the next general election. But he would like to see the country back in the bloc within his lifetime, and has suggested that a future Labour manifesto could promise a new referendum.
The changing mood is only part of the logic. A government searching for growth would naturally prioritise what is still its biggest trade partner. Geopolitics matter too. The UK’s bond with the United States is less reliable than it was.
Unsurprisingly, Brexit talk has swept through media in Britain and, to a lesser extent, in Europe. Burnham insists he will not get ahead of the public on this. His immediate concern, he says, is improving the current UK-EU relationship.
On Friday, Burnham will be in Brussels for the second UK-EU Summit – a vehicle established under Starmer to deepen post-Brexit cooperation.
Among the deals being worked on are a youth mobility scheme, an emissions trading agreement, and a food and drink trade deal.
“If he can reduce the red tape and the cost of sending cheese to Europe – and for us that means across the world – that would be a huge positive for us,” he said – although he was less certain which way he would vote in another referendum.
“Gosh, I genuinely don’t know. I think it would depend entirely on a critical view on the arguments that were presented at the time. A much more critical view than I had the first time around.”
It is an issue familiar to anyone who has lived through the Brexit years: the terms matter.
Former premier Theresa May used the motto, “Brexit means Brexit”. But the slogan was vague. What kind of Brexit? Hard? Soft? Norway Plus? Canada Plus?
There were many potential Brexits – as there might be many possible ways to rejoin.
In the most popular scenario, 58 percent said they would vote to rejoin if the UK stayed out of the euro, joined the border-free Schengen Zone, and kept its previous rebate from the EU budget. But if the UK lost the rebate, did not join Schengen, and adopted the euro, only 35 percent of people said they would be interested in EU membership.
Anticipating the battles ahead, two pro-Brexit campaign groups are relaunching under new names: Stay Out and Enough Official.
Burnham says he will begin talks with the EU about options for the long-term relationship after this week’s summit.

Flaming torches, blaring trumpets and wooden casks rolled down cobbles or carted on tractors set Lyon’s thoroughfares abuzz as costumed revellers led the city's annual wine parade. Drawing dense crowds, the festivities peaked with the theatrical uncorking of the season’s first bottles on stage, sparking music, dancing and cheers as the inaugural glasses were handed out.
Hailing from the hills just north of Lyon , Beaujolais Nouveau hits the shelves just weeks after the grapes are picked, sustaining a quintessential French autumn ritual. Celebrated globally on the third Thursday of November , the event heralds the exact stroke at which the new vintage may legally be sold — a light, fruit-forward wine meant for immediate enjoyment rather than long ageing.
What began as a local harvest marker is now a lively tribute to French winemaking heritage, bringing producers and townspeople shoulder to shoulder. Through its torchlit march and midnight pouring , Lyon once again turned the launch into an exuberant street festival.
